idiom_name: Quantity<U extends string> = number & brand + constructor/conversion functions
implementation_notes: TypeScript compiles to a runtime with one number type (see the handbook on everyday types), so the unit has to live in the type system: declare a generic Quantity<U extends string> as a branded intersection with a unique symbol and hide the assertions inside small constructor and conversion functions. Because the brand exists only for the checker, the runtime stays a plain number - zero cost - while adding metres to seconds becomes a compile error, and template literal types let compound units compose (Per<'km','m'> becomes 'km/m'). The classic class structure is replaced by constructors plus functions, so the guarantee is exactly as strong as the team's discipline in never passing a raw number where a branded one is expected.
pitfalls: JSON.parse, library results and untyped third-party APIs return plain numbers, so every boundary must re-apply a constructor (a schema/parser at the edge) or an unsafe as-assertion creeps in and quietly removes the guarantee.
Type errors and editor hovers show the brand intersection, which is unreadable without aliases and can leak into inferred signatures - keep the brand in one file with exported aliases.
There is no operator overloading, so all arithmetic must go through functions (add, per, times); teams that skip them end up writing casts inline, which is the anti-pattern.

variants.name: mathjs Unit objects from TypeScript
variants.implementation_notes: When the unit catalogue should be data rather than types - user-selectable units, imports, conversions driven by configuration - the pragmatic choice is mathjs with its type declarations: unit(3, 'km'), .to('m'), .toNumber('m') and a built-in catalogue including prefixes and affine temperature units. The unit checks then happen at run time and throw, so combine it with branded types at the seams inside your own code if compile-time safety is also wanted.
pitfalls: Unit checks are runtime errors, so a wrong dimension ships to production unless the tests cover the arithmetic paths.
Magnitudes default to number, so precision is lost in long chains unless BigNumber or Fraction values are used.
The type declarations are permissive (Unit is an interface), so nothing stops a plain object from being passed where a Unit is expected - validate at the boundary.
